The three new variables in UTAUT 2 are habit (HB), hedonic motivation (HM), and price value (PV). The text explains that UTAUT 2 was developed to enhance the explanatory power of the previous UTAUT version. The original UTAUT model consisted of effort expectancy (EE), performance expectancy (PE), facilitating condition (FC, and social influence (SI), and was highly used by scholars to predict intention to use new technology. However, it was criticized for its incapability to include an essential determinant of technology usage behaviour (Beh et al., 2019). To overcome that criticism, Venkatesh et al. (2012) added HB, HM, and PV. UTAUT 2 also focuses on post usage behaviour. The text states that various literature confirms UTAUT 2’s capability in explaining the continuance behaviour of technology usage, and that UTAUT 2 has better predictive power compared to other technological acceptance model (Rondan-Cataluña et al., 2015). Since Spotify Premium is considered a new technology in the music industry, it suits the concept in UTAUT, and the study uses the model to predict continuance behaviour of subscribing to Spotify Premium among university students in Malaysia. In this study, BI refers to the intention to continue subscribing to Spotify Premium.

Habit: Habit is described as the extent to which an individual believes a behaviour is a result of experience, so that the individual tends to perform it automatically based on learning from past experience (Venkatesh et al., 2012). According to Soares et al. (2020), habit could be influenced by past behaviour and personal experience in applying a particular system or product. If past experience produced favourable results, there is a high tendency to transform the particular behaviour into a habit. Past studies showed that habit produced a positive relationship with BI (Ameri et al., 2020; Nikolopoulou et al., 2020; Soares et al., 2020). The study therefore proposes H3: habit has positive effects on BI of Spotify Premium subscription.

Hedonic motivation: HM is the enjoyment or pleasure from technology usage (Venkatesh et al., 2012). This study defined HM as the enjoyment of Spotify Premium usage to enjoy music streaming. Based on research by Beh et al. (2019), HM showed a positive relationship with BI in the usage of smartwatches. Greece university students also showed that their HM had a positive relationship with BI concerning mobile phone usage (Nikolopoulou et al., 2020). The study therefore proposes H4: HM produced a positive effect on the BI of the Spotify Premium subscription.

Price value: PV refers to the relationship between consumers’ cognitive trade-off between the benefits gained versus the amount paid for the services (Venkatesh et al., 2012). The text states that Spotify Premium users will continue their subscription if the subscription is worth paying based on the services provided, and when there is beneficial experience from using Spotify Premium, or the received benefits are greater than the cost. Previously, it was discovered that PV has a positive relationship with the continued subscription of music streaming services (Lüders, 2020). Additionally, PV created a positive relationship with BI on the continued subscription to music streaming (Lüders, 2020) and continued use of mobile financial services (Rahman et al., 2020). The study therefore proposes H6: PV produced positive effects on the BI of Spotify Premium subscription.

**Summary**

Qualitex Company had used a special shade of green-gold color on the pads it makes and sells to dry cleaning firms for use on dry cleaning presses since the 1950’s. In 1989, Jacobson Products, a Qualitex rival, began selling its own press pads to dry cleaning firms and colored those pads a similar green-gold. In 1991, Qualitex registered the special green-gold color on press pads with the Patent and Trademark Office as a trademark, Registration No. 1,633,711 (Feb. 5, 1991). It then added a trademark-infringement count under 15 U.S.C. § 1114(1) to an unfair-competition claim under § 1125(a) in a lawsuit it had already filed challenging Jacobson’s use of the green-gold color.

Qualitex won in the District Court. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit set aside the judgment in Qualitex’s favor on the trademark-infringement claim because, in that court’s view, the Lanham Act does not permit Qualitex, or anyone else, to register “color alone” as a trademark. The Courts of Appeals had disagreed about whether the law recognizes the use of color alone as a trademark: NutraSweet imposed an absolute prohibition, while Owens-Corning allowed registration of pink for fiberglass insulation and Master Distributors declined to establish a per se prohibition. The Supreme Court therefore granted certiorari and held that there is no rule absolutely barring the use of color alone as a trademark. It reversed the Ninth Circuit.

**Act**

The Lanham Act supported the right to include color as a qualifying trademark.

**How the Act’s language supported the opinion**

The Court explained that both the language of the Lanham Act and the basic underlying principles of trademark law would seem to include color within the universe of things that can qualify as a trademark. Section 1127 describes trademarks in the broadest terms, saying that they “includ[e] any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof.” Because people might use as a “symbol” or “device” almost anything capable of carrying meaning, the Court said this language, read literally, is not restrictive. The Court noted that courts and the Patent and Trademark Office had already authorized particular shapes, such as marks a particular shape, such as the shape of a Coca-Cola bottle, a particular sound, such as NBC’s three chimes, and even a particular scent, such as plumeria blossoms on sewing thread. If a shape, a sound, and a fragrance can act as symbols, the Court asked why color could not do the same.

The statute also requires that a person “us[e]” or “inten[d] to use” the mark “to identify and distinguish his or her goods, including a unique product, from those manufactured or sold by others and to indicate the source of the goods, even if that source is unknown.” The Court acknowledged that a product’s color is unlike fanciful, arbitrary, or suggestive words or designs, which almost automatically signal a brand. An imaginary word like “Suntost” would immediately suggest a source, while orange jam’s orange color would not. But a color can still acquire “secondary meaning” over time. Customers may come to treat a particular color on a product or packaging, especially one that seems unusual in context, as signifying a brand. Once that happens, the color comes to identify and distinguish the goods and indicate their source, much as descriptive words such as “Trim” on nail clippers or “Car-Freshner” on deodorizer can do after acquiring secondary meaning.

Finally, the Court said it could not find in the basic objectives of trademark law any obvious theoretical objection to using color alone as a trademark when the color has attained secondary meaning and identifies a particular brand. Trademark law reduces customers’ costs of shopping and purchasing decisions, helps assure producers that they will receive financial and reputation-related rewards for desirable products, encourages quality production, and discourages competitors from selling inferior products by exploiting consumers’ inability quickly to evaluate quality. The Court emphasized that it is the source-distinguishing ability of a mark—not its ontological status as color, shape, fragrance, word, or sign—that allows it to serve these purposes. For that reason, the Court concluded that the Lanham Act’s language did not support an absolute bar against registering color alone as a trademark.

Under the Chapter V text, a transfer of personal data to a third country or international organisation may take place on the basis of a Commission decision that the destination ensures an adequate level of protection, and such a transfer shall not require any specific authorisation. The text sets out the impact as follows:

- General transfer condition: Article 44 states that any transfer of personal data which are undergoing processing or are intended for processing after transfer to a third country or to an international organisation shall take place only if, subject to the other provisions of this Regulation, the conditions laid down in this Chapter are complied with by the controller and processor, including for onward transfers of personal data from the third country or an international organisation to another third country or to another international organisation. All provisions in this Chapter shall be applied in order to ensure that the level of protection of natural persons guaranteed by this Regulation is not undermined.

- Basis for transfer: Article 45(1) states that a transfer of personal data to a third country or an international organisation may take place where the Commission has decided that the third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within that third country, or the international organisation in question ensures an adequate level of protection. It adds: “Such a transfer shall not require any specific authorisation.”

- Assessment criteria: When assessing the adequacy of the level of protection, the Commission shall, in particular, take account of:
  - the rule of law, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, relevant legislation, both general and sectoral, including concerning public security, defence, national security and criminal law and the access of public authorities to personal data, as well as the implementation of such legislation, data protection rules, professional rules and security measures, including rules for the onward transfer of personal data to another third country or international organisation which are complied with in that country or international organisation, case-law, as well as effective and enforceable data subject rights and effective administrative and judicial redress for the data subjects whose personal data are being transferred;
  - the existence and effective functioning of one or more independent supervisory authorities in the third country or to which an international organisation is subject, with responsibility for ensuring and enforcing compliance with the data protection rules, including adequate enforcement powers, for assisting and advising the data subjects in exercising their rights and for cooperation with the supervisory authorities of the Member States; and
  - the international commitments the third country or international organisation concerned has entered into, or other obligations arising from legally binding conventions or instruments as well as from its participation in multilateral or regional systems, in particular in relation to the protection of personal data.

- Adoption and review: After assessing the adequacy of the level of protection, the Commission may decide, by means of implementing act, that a third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within a third country, or an international organisation ensures an adequate level of protection within the meaning of paragraph 2. The implementing act shall provide for a mechanism for a periodic review, at least every four years, which shall take into account all relevant developments in the third country or international organisation. It shall specify its territorial and sectoral application and, where applicable, identify the supervisory authority or authorities referred to in point (b) of paragraph 2. It shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2).

- Ongoing monitoring: The Commission shall, on an ongoing basis, monitor developments in third countries and international organisations that could affect the functioning of decisions adopted pursuant to paragraph 3 of Article 45 and decisions adopted on the basis of Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC.

- Change, suspension or withdrawal: The Commission shall, where available information reveals, in particular following the review referred to in paragraph 3, that a third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within a third country, or an international organisation no longer ensures an adequate level of protection within the meaning of paragraph 2, to the extent necessary, repeal, amend or suspend the decision referred to in paragraph 3 by means of implementing acts without retro-active effect. Those implementing acts shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2). On duly justified imperative grounds of urgency, the Commission shall adopt immediately applicable implementing acts in accordance with the procedure referred to in Article 93(3).

- Consultations: The Commission shall enter into consultations with the third country or international organisation with a view to remedying the situation giving rise to the decision made pursuant to paragraph 5.

- Effect on other transfer routes: A decision pursuant to paragraph 5 is without prejudice to transfers of personal data to the third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within that third country, or the international organisation in question pursuant to Articles 46 to 49.

- Publication: The Commission shall publish in the Official Journal of the European Union and on its website a list of the third countries, territories and specified sectors within a third country and international organisations for which it has decided that an adequate level of protection is or is no longer ensured.

- Earlier Commission decisions under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC: Such decisions shall remain in force until amended, replaced or repealed by a Commission Decision adopted in accordance with paragraph 3 or 5 of Article 45.

- Where there is no adequacy decision: In the absence of a decision pursuant to Article 45(3), a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation only if the controller or processor has provided appropriate safeguards, and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available. The appropriate safeguards may be provided for, without requiring any specific authorisation from a supervisory authority, by:
  - a legally binding and enforceable instrument between public authorities or bodies;
  - binding corporate rules in accordance with Article 47;
  - standard data protection clauses adopted by the Commission in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2);
  - standard data protection clauses adopted by a supervisory authority and approved by the Commission pursuant to the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2);
  - an approved code of conduct pursuant to Article 40 together with binding and enforceable commitments of the controller or processor in the third country to apply the appropriate safeguards, including as regards data subjects' rights; or
  - an approved certification mechanism pursuant to Article 42 together with binding and enforceable commitments of the controller or processor in the third country to apply the appropriate safeguards, including as regards data subjects' rights.

  Subject to the authorisation from the competent supervisory authority, the appropriate safeguards may also be provided for, in particular, by:
  - contractual clauses between the controller or processor and the controller, processor or the recipient of the personal data in the third country or international organisation; or
  - provisions to be inserted into administrative arrangements between public authorities or bodies which include enforceable and effective data subject rights.

## What they measure

The core difference in what they measure is that **fundamental analysis evaluates intrinsic value**, while **technical analysis reviews historical price and volume data**.

**Fundamental analysis** is used in finance to evaluate the **intrinsic value—the real worth—of a security, sector, or economy**. It is used when scrutinizing **income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements** for a company’s stock. It is generally aimed at investors looking for **long-term value**, and those performing it are trying to calculate how much the company will make in the future against its present net value.

Its main tools include:

- **Financial statements**: income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement**, which provide an economic snapshot and help assess profitability, liquidity, and solvency.
- **Financial ratios, multiples, and other mathematical representations** of a firm’s financial health.
- **Economic indicators**, such as GDP growth, inflation, and unemployment rates, used to understand the economic environment in which a company operates.
- **Interest rates**, especially central bank interest rates; higher interest rates generally lead to lower stock prices, while lower rates boost stock prices.
- **News and events**, such as earnings reports, new contracts, and regulatory changes, which affect stock prices.
- **Qualitative information**, including management quality, industry cycles, competitive advantage, and other nonquantifiable factors that affect a company’s stock.

Investors use these tools to see whether a security is **undervalued or overvalued**.

**Technical analysis**, by contrast, evaluates financial assets—such as stocks, currencies, or commodities—by reviewing **historical price and volume data**. Unlike fundamental analysis, which focuses on intrinsic value, technical analysis examines the **volume and price of shares over time**. The text says that technical analysts start from the perspective that markets are inefficient and that price patterns and trends in market data can be exploited for potential profit.

Its main tools include:

- **Technical analysis indicators**: mathematical calculations based on price, volume, or open interest to predict future prices; generally based on momentum or mean reversion.
- **Volume analysis**: studies the number of shares, lots, or contracts traded in a security or market during a certain period.
- **Relative strength**: compares the performance of an asset to a benchmark to gauge its momentum.
- **Chart pattern analysis**: study of price movements that can pinpoint patterns suggesting future activity.
- **Candlestick pattern analysis**: a kind of financial chart used for price movements that could indicate investor sentiment, market trends, or reversals of those trends. Candlesticks have rectangular “bodies” showing opening and closing prices, with thin vertical lines called “wicks” or “shadows” showing high and low prices; bodies are often colored green/white for up moves and red/black for down moves.
- **Support and resistance**: horizontal lines drawn on a price chart to indicate where a security’s price will be unlikely to move beyond.
- **Trend analysis**: interpreting past and present moves in the market to predict future asset prices; historical prices and trading volume are the most often used.

Each element allows investors to analyze a share or market’s behavior.

---

## How they are used

The practical difference is that **fundamental analysis is generally used for long-term value judgments**, while **technical analysis is used to read price and volume behavior and support trading decisions**.

According to the text:

- Fundamental analysis can lead to **buying, holding, or selling** a security after determining whether it appears undervalued or overvalued.
- Technical analysis is used to **predict future prices**, identify patterns, interpret trends, assess momentum, understand sentiment, identify support and resistance levels, and time entry and exit points in trades.

---

## Criticisms and downsides of fundamental analysis

The text lists the following criticisms of fundamental analysis:

1. **Time-consuming**  
   It requires extensive research and data collection, which can be very time-intensive.

2. **Subjectivity**  
   Different analysts may interpret the same data differently, leading to the claim that results end up subjective.

3. **Information lag**  
   Financial reports and economic data are often released with a delay, potentially making the analysis outdated.

4. **Difficulty quantifying qualitative factors**  
   Aspects like management quality or brand value are hard to objectively measure.

5. **Assumption of market efficiency**  
   Fundamental analysis very often assumes that markets are efficient. Hence, long-term value—the prices on the stock market—will eventually match the stock’s underlying reality or intrinsic value. However, the long-term may never come.

6. **Long-term focus**  
   It may not be as useful for short-term trading decisions.

7. **Overlooking market sentiment**  
   It may not adequately account for investor psychology and market trends. It may miss important price trends and patterns that technical analysis might catch.

8. **Vulnerability to unexpected events**  
   Sudden geopolitical or economic events can quickly render fundamental analysis irrelevant.

These criticisms explain why fundamental analysis can be slower, more research-heavy, and less directly tied to short-term price movement than technical analysis.

---

## Criticisms and downsides of technical analysis

The text also presents several criticisms of technical analysis:

1. **It goes against the efficient market hypothesis**  
   One of the main criticisms is that technical analysis conflicts with the efficient market hypothesis. This theory suggests that stock prices already reflect all available information, making it impossible to consistently beat the market using any predefined strategy.

2. **Its advantages may disappear if everyone uses it**  
   Critics argue that even if technical analysis really worked, everyone would use it, and its advantages would quickly disappear.

3. **Subjectivity / non-objectivity**  
   Different analysts might interpret the same chart patterns differently, similar to seeing shapes in clouds, leading to inconsistent predictions.

4. **Risk of overfitting**  
   With so much financial data available today, there is a risk of finding patterns that seem meaningful but are actually just coincidences. The text compares this to flipping a coin 10 times, getting heads each time, and mistakenly concluding the coin is rigged.

5. **Data mining problem**  
   Patterns that seemed to work in the past may have no real predictive power for the future.

The text notes, however, that despite these criticisms, technical analysis remains popular among many traders and investors. It also gives counterarguments:

- Proponents say markets are not always perfectly efficient, and there is value in analyzing price trends and trading patterns.
- Some argue technical analysis may appear to work in some cases because of a **self-fulfilling prophecy**: if enough traders follow the same technical signals, their collective actions could actually move the market in the predicted direction, at least in the short term.
- Others point out that technical analysis can be a useful tool for understanding **market psychology and sentiment**. By studying price movements and trading volumes, analysts might gain insights into the emotions driving buying and selling pressure, which can be valuable for identifying resistance and support levels and timing entry and exit points in trades.

---

## Overall practical distinction

In practice, the text presents the two approaches as follows:

- **Fundamental analysis** focuses on intrinsic value, financial statements, economic conditions, interest rates, news, and qualitative factors, and is generally used for long-term valuation decisions.
- **Technical analysis** focuses on historical price, volume, chart patterns, indicators, support/resistance, and trends, and is used to predict future prices, read market behavior, understand sentiment, and time trades.

The text concludes that these criticisms highlight why some investors prefer technical analysis or combine both approaches.

In Brackeen v. Zinke, the plaintiffs—three states (Indiana, Louisiana, and Texas) and several private parties, primarily non-Indian couples who had adopted or wanted to adopt an Indian child—challenged parts of the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) and related regulations, including the 2016 Bureau of Indian Affairs Final Rule and certain funding provisions conditioned on ICWA compliance. The federal defendants, intervening tribes, and amicus curiae groups—including numerous federally recognized tribes, several Indian organizations, and a number of states—disputed the challenge and contended that the challenged laws and regulations were lawful.

## Arguments supporting the claim that ICWA is unconstitutional

### 1. Equal protection: race-based classification under the Fifth Amendment

The state and individual plaintiffs argued that ICWA violated the Fifth Amendment’s equal protection guarantees by using an impermissible race-based classification.

They focused on ICWA’s definition of an “Indian child”: any unmarried person under eighteen who is either a member of an Indian tribe or is both eligible for membership in an Indian tribe and the biological child of a member of an Indian tribe. The plaintiffs argued that this definition rests on ancestry rather than strictly on membership in a federally recognized tribe, and therefore amounts to racial classification.

Their argument relied on two Supreme Court precedent in two main ways:

- In Adarand Constructors v. Peña, the Supreme Court held that federal classifications based on race are subject to strict scrutiny, meaning the government must show that the classification serves a compelling government interest and is narrowly tailored to achieve that interest.
- In Cayetano, the Supreme Court recognized that “[a]ncestry can be a proxy for race” and may be subject to the same constitutional limitations as directly race-based classifications.

The plaintiffs contended that ICWA’s classification neither served a compelling interest nor was narrowly tailored.

The district court agreed with the plaintiffs that ICWA’s definition of Indian children was race-based rather than political. It viewed the case as more like Rice than like Mancari, because Mancari involved only tribe members rather than Indians eligible for tribal membership. Because the federal defendants had relied on the political-classification argument and had not fully briefed strict scrutiny, the court held that the race-based classification was not narrowly tailored, even assuming it served a compelling interest.

### 2. Nondelegation: Congress cannot delegate legislative power to tribes

The state plaintiffs argued that ICWA violated the nondelegation doctrine by giving Indian tribes the power to reorder ICWA’s placement preferences. The nondelegation doctrine generally prohibits Congress from delegating its core legislative powers to other government entities or to private parties.

The material notes that courts generally use the “intelligible principle” test to evaluate such delegations, and that this is a forgiving standard; the Supreme Court has not invalidated a statute on nondelegation grounds since 1935. It also notes that some have read Supreme Court jurisprudence as prohibiting Congress from delegating legislative power to private entities outside the government.

The district court relied on both understandings. It concluded that Congress had not provided a clear legal framework to guide the delegated authority under ICWA. It further agreed with the plaintiffs that the tribes’ authority to reorder adoption placement preferences was essentially legislative and could not be delegated. Even if that power could be delegated in some circumstances, the court reasoned that Indian tribes were akin to private entities that could not exercise delegated federal powers. The court was not receptive to the argument that Indian tribes are fundamentally distinct from other private parties, such as corporations, and should be treated differently in nondelegation analysis.

### 3. Anti-commandeering: ICWA forces states to carry out federal regulatory functions

The state plaintiffs argued that ICWA violated the anti-commandeering doctrine, which is rooted in the Constitution’s allocation of power between the federal government and the states. That doctrine prohibits Congress from forcing state political branches to perform regulatory functions on the federal government’s behalf.

The plaintiffs claimed that ICWA requires state courts and executive agencies to apply federal standards and directives in policy areas normally reserved to non-federal jurisdiction, such as adoptions, foster care policies, and other child custody issues.

The district court accepted this argument. It held that ICWA commandeered state courts and agencies into applying federal directives in areas traditionally governed by states. It tersely rejected the federal government’s counterargument that ICWA was instead an exercise of Congress’s “plenary and exclusive” authority over Indian tribes.

### 4. Administrative Procedure Act challenge to the 2016 BIA Final Rule

The plaintiffs also challenged the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ 2016 Final Rule under the Administrative Procedure Act. The rule sought to create uniformity in ICWA’s application across states and, among other things, clarified when “good cause” exists for circumventing ICWA’s placement preferences.

The district court took a two-part approach:

1. It held that any regulation implementing portions of ICWA that it had already declared unconstitutional should be struck down.
2. In the alternative, it held that the 2016 rule exceeded the scope of BIA’s statutory regulatory authority. In the court’s view, the rule “clarified” a provision that was not ambiguous and did not need clarification. Because the court considered the underlying statutory provision unambiguous, it gave no deference to the agency’s determination that the regulation was necessary.

### 5. Indian Commerce Clause

The plaintiffs also claimed that ICWA exceeded Congress’s legislative powers under the Indian Commerce Clause. The district court purported to grant this claim, but only as an extension of its anti-commandeering ruling. Its reasoning was that Congress’s power over Indian commerce cannot be used to commandeer the states.

### 6. Substantive due process

The individual plaintiffs raised substantive due process claims, arguing that ICWA infringed their fundamental rights of custody and family togetherness as foster or would-be adoptive parents of Indian children.

The district court rejected these claims. It observed that the Supreme Court had not applied the fundamental rights of custody and keeping families together to foster families, and it declined to extend those rights to the individual plaintiffs challenging ICWA.

### 7. Policy argument from challengers

The material also notes that at least one advocacy group has made challenging ICWA part of its core mission. That group claims that Native American children are being harmed because ICWA hinders the ability of non-Native persons to adopt them.

---

## Arguments opposing the claim that ICWA is unconstitutional

### 1. Political, not racial, classification

The federal defendants, intervening tribes, and amici argued that ICWA’s distinctions are political rather than racial. They emphasized longstanding Supreme Court jurisprudence holding that the federal government’s relationship with federally recognized Indian tribes is based on political categorizes people by their political status, not by race.

A central example they cited was Mancari, in which the Supreme Court upheld a Bureau of Indian Affairs employment preference for members of federally recognized tribes. The Court treated that preference as a political classification because it singled out members of tribal entities that have a unique relationship with the federal government.

The opponents of the unconstitutionality claim also invoked the Supreme Court’s observation that “[l]iterally every piece of legislation dealing with Indian tribes” is “explicitly designed to help only Indians,” and that treating such legislation as racial discrimination would jeopardize “the solemn commitment of the Government toward the Indians.”

### 2. Plenary federal power over Indian affairs

The material explains that prior courts had upheld special rules for Indian children by relying on Congress’s “plenary” authority over Indian affairs, derived principally from the Indian Commerce Clause and the Treaty Power. Those courts concluded that the distinction between Indians and non-Indians was not an impermissible race-based classification, but a recognition of the unique political status of Indian tribes.

### 3. Congressional purpose and protective design of ICWA

Opponents of the unconstitutionality claim pointed to the historical and statutory purpose of ICWA. In 1978, Congress recognized that an “alarmingly high percentage of Indian families” were being broken up by often-unwarranted removal of their children by nontribal entities, placing many of those children in non-Indian foster and adoptive homes.

Citing its responsibility to protect and preserve Indian tribes, Congress passed ICWA to protect Indian children as vital to the tribes’ continued existence. ICWA was designed to do two primary things:

1. set standards for placing Indian children with foster or adoptive families; and  
2. help tribes establish child and family programs.

### 4. Narrow tailoring and best interests of children

On appeal, the federal government argued that ICWA protects tribe members and their families, including not-yet-enrolled children of tribal members, and that it is narrowly tailored to protect the best interests of those children.

The government also suggested that if the Fifth Circuit agreed that strict scrutiny applied, the case should be remanded to the district court for full briefing on that issue.

### 5. Precedent against invalidating ICWA

The material notes that, although ICWA had been challenged repeatedly over the past 40 years, including on race-based grounds, direct challenges to ICWA generally had been unsuccessful before Brackeen, with perhaps one limited but notable exception.

In Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, popularly known as the Baby Veronica case, the Supreme Court did not invalidate ICWA. In a 5-4 decision, it limited the range of circumstances in which certain ICWA provisions might apply. The Court held that several ICWA provisions were inapplicable if the parent seeking to invoke them had never had legal or physical custody of the Indian child. In that case, the Indian father—who had never had custody of his daughter—could not invoke ICWA to block her adoption.

The Court also held that ICWA’s placement preferences were relevant only if multiple parties actually sought to adopt the Indian child. Because only one party—a non-Indian couple—was trying to adopt the child in the Baby Veronica case, ICWA’s placement preferences could not prevent the adoption from being finalized.

The material further notes that the Ninth Circuit dismissed another constitutional challenge to ICWA as moot because the would-be adoptive parents had completed their adoptions, and that the Supreme Court had so far declined to hear other cases challenging ICWA.

### 6. Procedural objections on appeal

The federal defendants also argued on appeal that each aspect of the district court’s decision was “unprecedented and in conflict with binding authority.” They renewed challenges to the plaintiffs’ standing and argued that ICWA’s severability clause meant the district court’s ruling should have been narrower in any event.

### 7. Tribal sovereignty concern

Finally, the material notes that ICWA’s supporters fear that challengers are jeopardizing longstanding principles underlying tribal sovereignty while “[c]loaking [their] efforts in the language of civil rights.”

**Mechanism of action**

Amoxicillin belongs to the class of beta-lactam antimicrobials. Beta-lactams bind to penicillin-binding proteins, inhibiting transpeptidation — a crucial step in cell wall synthesis involving cross-linking. This action activates autolytic enzymes in the bacterial cell wall, resulting in cell wall lysis and bacterial cell destruction. This mechanism is described as bactericidal killing. Amoxicillin administration can be combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, such as clavulanic acid or sulbactam. These inhibitors function by irreversibly binding to the catalytic site of the organism's beta-lactamase enzyme, preventing resistance to the original beta-lactam ring of amoxicillin. Although these inhibitors lack inherent bactericidal activity, their combination with amoxicillin may broaden its spectrum to include organisms producing the beta-lactamase enzyme.

**Potential side effects**

Although generally well-tolerated, amoxicillin may lead to common gastrointestinal symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Additional adverse drug reactions include:

- **Nephrotoxicity:** amoxicillin may cause crystalluria and interstitial nephritis.  
- **Hypersensitivity reactions:** amoxicillin has the potential to cause hypersensitivity reactions categorized as type I, II, III, or IV. Differentiating between a type-I and type-IV reaction is crucial due to varying danger levels. A type-I hypersensitivity reaction involves an IgE-mediated response in sensitized patients, inducing widespread histamine release, resulting in an urticarial-like pruritic rash or severe anaphylaxis. In contrast, a type-IV hypersensitivity reaction is not mediated by histamine release and typically presents as a more papular or morbilliform rash, often without itching. Almost all patients receiving amoxicillin inadvertently for infectious mononucleosis may develop a maculopapular rash attributed to a type IV–mediated hypersensitivity reaction. Reactions of this type are not associated with anaphylaxis.  
- **Hepatotoxicity:** cases of idiosyncratic liver injury have been reported in individuals receiving amoxicillin. The associated with a hepatocellular pattern characterized by significant elevations in aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT), with minimal increases in alkaline phosphatase. Most patients experience rapid recovery upon withdrawal of amoxicillin. The cause of liver injury associated with amoxicillin use is attributed to hypersensitivity. Although rare, cases of acute liver failure and vanishing bile duct syndrome have been reported.  
- **Postmarketing gastrointestinal effects:** black hairy tongue, pseudomembranous colitis, and hemorrhagic colitis.  
- **Neurological effects:** reversible hyperactivity, agitation, anxiety, insomnia, confusion, convulsions, and aseptic meningitis.  
- **Dermatological effects:** serum sickness-like reactions, erythematous maculopapular rashes, exfoliative dermatitis, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and hypersensitivity vasculitis.

Based on the provided material, a laminotomy is the removal of a small portion of the lamina to decompress one side (left or right) of the spinal canal. It leaves most of the lamina intact. More broadly, spinal decompression surgery is performed to relieve symptoms related to compression of the spinal cord or its roots. Those symptoms may include back or neck pain and radiating limb pain, called radiculopathy. Spinal nerve compression symptoms can include pain, altered sensations, muscle weakness or dysfunction, and even gait abnormalities. These symptoms can be caused by a wide variety of conditions. In some conditions, such as cervical spinal stenosis that leads to cervical myelopathy, symptoms may appear in the arms, hands, legs or feet, and/or there may be balance problems or incontinence issues, such as bowel dysfunction or unexpected need to urinate. A rapid onset of these symptoms can indicate cauda equina syndrome, which can cause paralysis and other serious problems if not addressed in a timely manner. Pain and other symptoms treated by these surgeries are most common in the lower back (lumbar spine), followed by the neck (cervical spine). Symptoms in the upper back (thoracic spine) are possible but less common because it is the most stable part of the spine, partly because it is connected to the rib cage. Neuropathies may involve numbness or a “pins and needles” tingling sensation and can cause weakness or instability, primarily in the lower back.

Every type of spinal decompression modifies or removes bone, spinal disc or soft tissues that are causing compression of a nerve. The techniques vary according to which tissues are causing the compression.

Several types of spine decompression surgery performed at HSS include laminectomy, laminotomy, laminoplasty, discectomy and microdiscectomy, among others. Lumbar decompression surgery may be used to address problems in the lower back, such as lumbar laminectomy, laminotomy, or microdiscectomy.

Laminectomy is the removal in one or more vertebrae of the lamina, the bony roof over the spinal canal. This decompresses both sides, left and right, of the canal. Laminotomy is removal of a small portion of the lamina to decompress one side, left or right, of the canal. This leaves most of the lamina intact. Microsurgical laminoplasty is a minimally invasive surgical decompression technique that uses small incisions viewed through an operating microscope; it involves reshaping part of a vertebral lamina. Microdiscectomy, also known as spinal microdecompression surgery, is a minimally invasive spine procedure commonly performed on patients who have sciatica and/or a herniated disc in the lumbar section of the spine. Using muscle-sparing incisions, it removes portions of a herniated disc that is putting pressure on the spinal nerve and causing pain. Minimally invasive lumbar discectomy, also known as endoscopic percutaneous disc removal, is similar to microdiscectomy and uses a scope to make very small incisions in the skin, through which a portion of the herniated disc that is compressing spinal nerves is removed.

Some decompression surgeries may require the addition of a fusion procedure simultaneously. This depends on the type of disease being treated and the technique being used. This includes lumbar decompressions, such as lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) techniques, which may indirectly decompress the spine, or cervical decompressions, such as anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF surgery), which are dependent on the differential anatomy of the spine.

Decompression surgery can be a good option for people who have back or neck pain and/or neuropathies due to nerve compression caused by a herniated disc, spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, and for whom nonsurgical methods such as physical therapy, epidural steroid injections or pain management regimens have failed to provide relief.

Most spinal decompression surgeries will be performed under general anesthesia, with the patient completely unconscious. Some modern techniques allow for spinal surgery under regional anesthesia, either spinal or epidural anesthesia. These techniques allow patients to breathe on their own without mechanical assistance. They may reduce complications associated with general anesthesia but are not widely available and may be performed on a case-by-case basis.

In many cases, patients undergoing decompressions such as a laminectomy, discectomy, or microdiscectomy can go home the same day. This is often the case with a laminectomy, microdiscectomy, and there is research to suggest that even multilevel ACDF surgeries may be safely done on an outpatient basis. Some patients having spinal decompression may need to stay one or more nights, including those who have chronic diseases or sleep problems. Some patients requiring a spinal fusion may stay overnight and return home one or two days after surgery. Rarely, a patient may need to stay longer. Some decompression spine surgeries may be planned as an ambulatory outpatient procedure, but then converted to an overnight stay to monitor the patient. In one study of more than 1,000 patients who underwent an ambulatory one- or two-level lumbar decompression, 58% ended up staying over at least one night.

At HSS, patients are encouraged to walk the same day of most decompression surgeries. Depending on the specific procedure and other factors, patients generally are able to return to work between two and four weeks after surgery. Some patients who have a microdiscectomy decompression may be able to return to work after less than two weeks.

The recovery time for decompression surgery alone is generally faster compared to procedures that include a fusion. Because of the wide range of decompression surgery types and the number of spinal levels addressed with surgery, there is likewise some variability in recovery duration. There is recent evidence that microdiscectomy patients can return to physical therapy and low impact aerobic exercise within four weeks of surgery. Patients undergoing laminectomy procedure can expect surgery pain to ease within two to four weeks of surgery and starting physical therapy and other activities by about six weeks. Fusion procedures likewise are highly variable and recovery times are prolonged, approaching three to six months before patients can return to exercise or sports activities. Precise success rates of spinal decompression surgery can be difficult to calculate due to the wide variety of procedures, severity of spinal conditions, and the age and health of individual patients. Patients can expect a significant decrease in their pain and an improvement in their overall function. Conferring with your surgeon regarding your procedure and expected recovery is advised.

- Behavioral research suggests people have biases in predictable patterns and use heuristics, or mental shortcuts, to make decisions quickly; these heuristics can sometimes lead to choices that make the decisionmaker worse off financially.
- In the life-cycle model, households may adjust their savings rate during working years based on interest rates, investment returns, life expectancy, Social Security or pension benefits, and other relevant factors. Evidence exists that some households adjust retirement planning based on these types of factors.
- Research suggests that choice architecture, or how financial decisions are framed, can affect consumer decisionmaking, and how saving and investment options are framed may help some people make better retirement decisions. The number, order, and structure of options, as well as the process around the choice, can change decisions for many people.
- People can be influenced, or anchored, by an initial number, even if it is unrelated to their next choice. In retirement savings, the automatic contribution rate in 401(k)s and the percent of salary at which employers provide maximum matches may be anchors that influence how much a person decides to save.
- People can also be influenced by defaults established in how a decision is framed. Employees are more likely to be enrolled in a 401(k) plan if an employer defaults them into it than if they actively need to make a choice to participate.
- When making decisions, people often find it difficult to navigate complexity, such as many choices to choose from or items to consider. In retirement savings plans, more investment fund options can sometimes lead to procrastination or failure to make a decision, while some research suggests fewer choices might lead to better retirement investment decisions.
- People tend to naively make diversification choices when making allocation decisions. For example, some people choose to spread investments evenly across available funds, whether or not that is financially appropriate for their situation.
- Present bias occurs when people put more value on having something now rather than in the future, even when there is a large benefit for waiting. In retirement, people tend to prefer lump sums over annuities, and research suggests people with more present bias tend to save less for retirement.
- Even when people decide they should save for the future or choose a retirement plan, self-control and procrastination may prevent them from following their intentions. These human biases might lead consumers to make nonoptimal financial decisions, such as undersaving.
- Firms may take advantage of consumers' biases to attract them, for example by developing marketing materials that emphasize high past investment return rates. Product features may also be developed to take advantage of present bias or self-control mistakes, and less knowledgeable retirement savers' decisionmaking might be more sensitive to choice architecture biases.
- Some research suggests that choice architecture environments can make retirement more salient, and annual consumer disclosures that project future retirement income may lead to more retirement savings. Some research also suggests that preference checklists listing factors such as perceived health, life expectancy, and risk of outliving one's resources may improve retirement decisionmaking.

Overall, the text identifies several key competitive factors among video streaming services. First, price is central. Subscription- or transaction-based services can compete by charging less than rivals. Live-TV streaming services may be cheaper than MVPD packages depending on channels. Some MVPDs responded with cheaper smaller-channel plans and improved set-top boxes that include services such as Netflix. Some live-TV streaming services advertise no hidden equipment-rental or cancellation fees and no annual contracts. Month-to-month signups appeal to some consumers but allow price increases, as shown when YouTube TV added eight channels and raised its price from fifty dollars to sixty-five dollars per month in 2020. Second, content matters. Services offering live TV generally cost more than video-on-demand-only services because licensing television network rights is costly. Expanding the number of networks attracts users but raises operating costs. Video-on-demand services license some previously shown movies and shows, which tends to lower licensing costs. Third, exclusive and original programming is important. Early streamers relied on licensed previously broadcast content, but later commissioned originals. Originals increased the importance of content and reduced dependence on network licensing agreements. Awards and nominations, such as those received by Netflix, Hulu, and other platforms, reflect the increased importance of content. Fourth, ownership structure affects competition. Companies owning studios and networks may reserve popular titles for their platforms, such as Warner Brothers shows on HBO and HBO Max, NBCUniversal shows on Peacock, or The Simpsons on Disney+. This can restrict competitors' access to popular content and make market entry harder because entrants may invest heavily in producing or licensing content before serving customers. Finally, streaming services differ from television networks and theaters because they offer multiple programs rather than one at a time. This lets them target various user groups, increasing competition for video content and creating opportunities for content creators.

## Symptoms

According to the passage, the hallmark asthma symptoms include:

- Shortness of breath

During physical examination, widespread, high-pitched wheezes are described as a characteristic finding associated with asthma. However, the passage states that wheezing is not specific to asthma and is typically absent between acute exacerbations.

Findings suggestive of a severe asthma exacerbation include:

- Tachypnea  
- Tachycardia  
- Prolonged expiratory phase  
- Reduced air movement  
- Difficulty speaking in complete sentences or phrases  
- Discomfort when lying supine due to breathlessness  
- Adopting a “tripod position”  

Additional indicators of a severe asthma attack include:

- Use of the accessory muscles of breathing during inspiration  
- Pulsus paradoxus  

The passage also mentions extrapulmonary findings that may support the diagnosis of asthma, such as:

- Posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning

The passage says that wheezing caused by viral infections—particularly respiratory syncytial virus and human rhinovirus—may predispose infants and young children to develop asthma later in life.

- Early-life exposure to air pollution, including combustion by-products from gas-fired appliances and indoor fires  
- Obesity  
- Early puberty  

### Adulthood

For adult-onset asthma, the passage identifies the most significant risk factors as:

- Tobacco smoke  
- Occupational exposure  
- Rhinitis or atopy  

It also states that studies suggest a modest increase in asthma incidence among postmenopausal women taking hormone replacement therapy.

### Factors that can contribute to asthma and airway hyperreactivity

The passage lists the following as factors that can contribute to asthma and airway hyperreactivity:

- Exposure to environmental allergens such as house dust mites, animal allergens especially from cats and dogs, cockroach allergens, and fungi  
- Physical activity or exercise  
- Conditions such as hyperventilation, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and chronic sinusitis

The passage describes aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, or AERD, as a condition characterized by a combination of:

Patients with AERD present with upper and lower respiratory tract symptoms after ingesting aspirin or NSAIDs that inhibit cyclooxygenase-1, or COX-1. The passage says this condition arises from dysregulated arachidonic acid metabolism and overproduction of leukotrienes involving the 5-lipoxygenase and cyclooxygenase pathways. It affects approximately 7% of adults with asthma.

The passage says there are a number of causes and risk factors that can bring on pancreatitis, though it often seems to hit out of the blue.

**Signs and symptoms**

The classic signs listed are:

- Hunched back  
- Repeated vomiting, either several times within a few hours or periodically over several days  
- Pain or distention of the abdomen, with the dog appearing uncomfortable or bloated  
- Diarrhea  
- Loss of appetite  
- Dehydration  
- Weakness/lethargy  
- Fever  

It says that if your dog exhibits one of these signs, and only infrequently, monitor your dog. If your dog exhibits multiple signs at once, and repeatedly, a call to the veterinarian quickly is vital.

Dehydration is due to greater fluid loss than fluid intake. Diarrhea or vomiting can cause dehydration, but those signs together will cause a greater fluid deficit and dehydration because the dog’s fluid input, drinking, cannot keep up with the fluid losses. If the diarrhea becomes bloody, the condition worsens and the dehydration can become an emergency. Dehydration is a serious condition that can lead to death; it is an emergency and requires immediate veterinary care. Any lethargic dog who is not drinking water or cannot hold water down should be suspect of dehydration and examined by a veterinarian. Dry mucous membranes, such as gums, may be a quick way of assessing dehydration, but when in doubt, consult with your veterinarian. Blood in a dog’s stool indicates a loose and significant inflammatory response requiring a veterinarian’s attention, though it can be caused by a multitude of factors, from ulceration to parasites.

**Breeds and risk factors**

Certain breeds or types of dogs have been associated with higher risks of pancreatitis, such as Miniature Schnauzers and some of the smaller toy and terrier breeds. There may, in some cases, be a genetic predisposition.

Causes and risk factors listed include:

- A high-fat diet — described as a major cause, especially for a dog who gets one large helping of fatty food in one sitting  
- A history of dietary indiscretion, described as a medical term for saying your dog will eat anything  
- Obesity  
- Hypothyroidism, or other endocrine diseases  
- Severe blunt trauma  
- Diabetes mellitus  
- Certain medications or other toxins, including cholinesterase inhibitors, calcium, potassium bromide, phenobarbital, l-asparaginase, estrogen, salicylates, azathioprine, thiazide diuretics, and vinca alkaloids  

The passage also says human food is especially dangerous, though even high-fat dog food may cause pancreatitis. Owner vigilance is particularly required around holidays and other festive occasions, because they can bring well-meaning guests who slip your dog a fatty piece of lamb, or leave a tray of buttery cookies within reach of an eager muzzle. The day after Thanksgiving is one of the busiest days of the year for pancreatitis-related emergency vet visits. If your dog is showing any signs of abdominal pain, the worst thing to do is feed him a fatty diet, and giving your dog table scraps is not advisable.

**Testing and diagnosis**

For diagnosis, the passage lists:

- Your dog’s medical history  
- Blood tests to measure pancreatic enzymes  
- Physical examination, including stomach, gums, heart, and temperature  
- Radiographs or ultrasound, to rule out other causes  
- Fine needle aspiration of the pancreas  

As the Merck Veterinary Manual notes, as with any disease, no test should be used in isolation for diagnosis, and all clinical findings should be used in conjunction to arrive at the most appropriate diagnosis.

The discussion identifies two closely related exceptions to the knock-and-announce rule: exigent circumstances and no-knock warrants. Their justifications are similar and are sometimes described interchangeably, because both typically involve a risk that knocking and announcing would endanger officers or result in the destruction of evidence. A key difference is temporal. With no-knock warrants, officers have anticipated exigent circumstances before searching, and have asked for pre-search judicial approval to enter without knocking; no-knock warrants provide explicit authority for judges to grant so-called no-knock entry in the warrant itself, upon a finding of certain factual predicates. Under the exigent-circumstances exception, by contrast, the justification may arise as late as when officers are at the door, based on reasonable suspicion that knocking and announcing would be dangerous, futile, or destructive to the purposes of the investigation. Exigent circumstances must be based on the particular circumstances of each case, and may not amount to a blanket exception to the knock-and-announce requirement for entire categories of criminal activity. The Supreme Court rejected the assertion that police officers are never required to knock and announce their presence when executing a search warrant in a felony drug investigation.

Some courts have concluded that no-knock warrants shield officers from responsibility for independently assessing the existence of exigent circumstances at the time of entry. To the extent that is true, no-knock warrants could permit no-knock entry where the exigent-circumstances exception would not—for example, in an instance where the factors that justified the no-knock warrant are no longer present at the time of entry. Relatedly, if a valid no-knock warrant provides such a shield against the responsibility of reassessing exigent circumstances at the time of entry, it could limit the availability of civil lawsuits as a remedy where officers disregard knock and announce requirements pursuant to a no-knock warrant, but exigent circumstances no longer exist at the time of entry.

The text also states that a number of states have statutes that authorize magistrate judges to grant no-knock warrants in certain circumstances. Although a federal statute previously authorized no-knock warrants for certain drug searches, Congress repealed it. As a result, the legal status of federal no-knock search warrants is unsettled, although federal officers do sometimes employ no-knock warrants or act pursuant to no-knock warrants issued by state courts when serving on joint state-federal task forces. One unresolved question is whether federal courts have authority to issue no-knock warrants in the absence of a statute expressly providing that power, as federal courts possess only that power authorized by Constitution and statute. The DOJ has concluded that federal courts are authorized to do so, in large part because the federal rule governing search warrants has been broadly interpreted by courts in other contexts to include specific searches that it does not expressly authorize. From a Fourth Amendment standpoint, the Supreme Court has indicated some approval of the practice of allowing magistrates to issue no-knock warrants when sufficient cause to do so can be demonstrated ahead of time, assuming that the practice does not amount to a blanket exception to knock and announce. In one sense, the legal vitality of federal no-knock warrants may be of limited practical significance, because federal law enforcement officers may still be permitted to enter a home without knocking and announcing if exigent circumstances are present.

Fentanyl has become increasingly prevalent in the U.S. drug supply, creating an unprecedented overdose death rate and other devastating consequences. Against that backdrop, the text says people with opioid use disorder urgently need treatment not just to protect them from overdosing but also to help them achieve recovery, while highly effective medications such as buprenorphine and methadone remain underused.

It singles out methadone because, amid this crisis, it may hold unique clinical advantages in the age of fentanyl. Growing evidence suggests methadone is as safe and effective as buprenorphine for patients who use fentanyl. In a 2020 naturalistic follow-up study, 53% of patients admitted to methadone treatment who tested positive for fentanyl at intake were still in treatment a year later, compared with 47% of patients who tested negative. Almost all (99%) of those retained in treatment achieved remission. An earlier study similarly found that 89% of patients who tested positive for fentanyl at methadone treatment intake and remained in treatment at 6 months achieved abstinence. Methadone may even be preferable for patients considered at high risk for leaving OUD treatment and overdosing on fentanyl. Emerging comparative effectiveness evidence from British Columbia showed that people with OUD given buprenorphine/naloxone when initiating treatment were 60% more likely to discontinue treatment than those who received methadone.

The text also emphasizes that only a fraction of people who could benefit from medication treatment for OUD receive it, due to structural and attitudinal barriers. A study using 2019 National Survey on Drug Use and Health data, described as pre-pandemic, found that only slightly more than a quarter (27.8%) of people who needed OUD treatment in the past year had received medication to treat their disorder. A year into the pandemic, in 2021, the proportion had dropped to just 1 in 5.

Some access expansions have already occurred. In 2021, HHS advanced what the text calls the most comprehensive Overdose Prevention Strategy to date, and under that strategy, in 2023, HHS eliminated the X-waiver requirement for buprenorphine. But the text says that in the fentanyl era, expanded access to methadone too is essential, even though there are even greater attitudinal and structural barriers with this medication. People in methadone treatment must regularly visit an opioid treatment programs, face stigma from their community and from providers, and people in rural areas may have difficulty accessing or sticking with treatment if they live far from an OTP. The U.S. still restricts methadone prescribing and dispensing more than most other countries, and worries about methadone’s safety and diversion have made some physicians and policymakers hesitant about lowering guardrails.

The text supports looser access by pointing to evidence from relaxed rules. SAMHSA’s changes to 42 CFR Part 8 on January 30, 2024 made permanent the increased take-home doses of methadone established in March 2020 during the pandemic, along with other provisions aimed at broadening access, such as the ability to initiate methadone treatment via telehealth. Studies show telehealth is associated with an increased likelihood of receiving MOUD, and take-home doses increase treatment retention. The changes implemented during the pandemic have not been associated with adverse outcomes.

Other data cited in the text also counter concerns. An analysis of CDC overdose death data from January 2019 to August 2021 found that the percentage of overdose deaths involving methadone relative to all drug overdose deaths declined from 4.5% to 3.2%. Expanded methadone access was not associated with significant changes in urine drug test results, emergency department visits, or increases in overdose deaths involving methadone. An analysis of poison control center reports found a small increase in intentional methadone exposures in the year after federal methadone regulations were loosened, but no significant increases in exposure severity, hospitalizations, or deaths.

Patients themselves reported benefits. Patients at one California OTP reported increased autonomy and treatment engagement. Patients at three rural OTPs in Oregon reported increased self-efficacy, strengthened recovery, and reduced interpersonal conflict.

The text does not ignore risks. Methadone treatment is not without risks. Some studies have found elevated rates of overdose during the induction and stabilization phase of maintenance treatment, potentially due to starting at too high a dose, escalating too rapidly, or drug interactions. But it also notes that although greatly increased prescribing of methadone for pain two decades ago was associated with diversion and a rise in methadone overdoses, overdoses declined after 2006, along with methadone’s use as an analgesic, even as its use for OUD increased. Most methadone overdoses are associated with diversion and, less often, prescription for chronic pain; currently, 70% of methadone overdoses involve other opioids, like fentanyl, or benzodiazepines.

Models outside OTPs also do not support fears of added harm. Recent trials of pharmacy-based dispensing and care models in settings other than OTPs have not supported concerns that making methadone more widely available will lead to harms like overdose. In two feasibility studies, stably maintained patients from OTPs in Baltimore, Maryland, and Raleigh, North Carolina, who received their methadone from a local pharmacy found the model highly satisfactory, with no positive urine screens, adverse events, or safety issues. An older pilot study in New Mexico found that prescribing methadone in a doctor’s office and dispensing it in a community pharmacy, as well as methadone treatment delivered by social workers, produced better outcomes than standard care in an OTP for a sample of stably maintained female methadone patients.

The text also addresses the role of counseling. Critics sometimes argue methadone should not be offered without accompanying behavioral treatment, but data suggest counseling is not essential. In wait-list studies, methadone treatment was effective at reducing opioid use on its own, and patients stayed in treatment. However, counseling may have benefits or even be indispensable for some patients to help them improve their psychosocial functioning and reduce other drug use, and how to personalize the intensity and level of support needed requires further investigation.

More research is still needed on optimal methadone dosing for patients with high opioid tolerance due to fentanyl use, and on induction protocols for these patients; it is possible that escalation to a therapeutic dose may need to be more rapid.

The text also notes that over the past two decades, the opioid crisis has accelerated the integration of addiction care in the U.S. with mainstream medicine. Yet methadone, the oldest and still one of the most effective medications in the OUD treatment toolkit, remains siloed.
